lead: A wing carries lift with a thin box: skin panels, stringers, ribs and two spars. The box takes bending as compression in the top skin and tension in the bottom skin, and takes torsion as shear in the closed cell between the spars. A fuselage is a stiffened tube: frames and longerons hold a thin skin in shape and carry bending, shear and cabin pressure. Learn the members, their spacing, and how a load travels from skin to root joint. The later work on bending of thin-walled beams and on shear flow assumes this layout.
prereq: You need: Structural components of aircraft and their functions for the load-path idea, and Monocoque and semi-monocoque construction for why the skin needs a skeleton behind it.

sections.h3: Two spars make a torsion box

blocks.text: A spar is a spanwise beam running from root to tip. Most wings have a front spar near the leading edge and a rear spar further back. Each spar has a thin vertical web and two spar caps: spanwise flanges at the top and bottom of the web. Bending bends the wing up, so the top skin and top caps shorten and the bottom skin and bottom caps stretch. The caps take this axial load. The webs take shear.

The skin between the front and rear spar, together with the two webs, closes a cell called the torsion box. A closed cell resists twisting far better than an open sheet, because the shear has a continuous path all round the loop. The box sits in the deepest part of the aerofoil for two reasons: the torsional stiffness of a closed thin-walled cell grows with the square of the area it encloses, and the bending stiffness grows with the depth between the top and bottom skins.

blocks.where: w<sub>box</sub> is the torsion box width in m; x<sub>front</sub> and x<sub>rear</sub> are the front and rear spar positions as a fraction of chord (0 to 1); c is the chord in m.

blocks.text: Shear force and bending moment along the span are worked out in Shear force and bending moment distribution on wings; the shear flow inside this closed box comes later, with torsion of closed sections (the Bredt-Batho theory).

A rib is a chordwise member: it runs from the leading edge to the trailing edge, crossing the box. Ribs hold the aerofoil section, support the skin and stringers, and pass panel loads into the spars. They also carry local loads in: engine mounts, landing gear, flap and aileron hinges all feed the wing through a few ribs. Ribs sit at a regular pitch, for example 0.45 m on a small wing.

A stringer is a small spanwise stiffener on the inside face of the skin, closely spaced. Stringers stop the thin skin from buckling, and together with the skin they act as the upper and lower flanges in bending.

items: Aerodynamic pressure on the top skin loads that panel.
The panel passes the load to the stringers running spanwise.
Stringers hand the load to the ribs at each crossing.
Ribs carry it chordwise to the front and rear spar web.
Spars carry it spanwise to the root joint, which hands it to the fuselage frames.

blocks.text: The leading edge, ahead of the front spar, and the trailing edge, behind the rear spar, are lighter structures. They keep the profile shape, carry the slats, flaps and ailerons, and take little of the wing bending.
The fuselage is a semi-monocoque shell: skin, frames, longerons and bulkheads. Each has one job.

items: Frames are transverse rings, set at a regular pitch along the cabin. They keep the cross-section round, support the skin against buckling, and carry the hoop load from cabin pressure together with the skin.

Stringers are many light lengthwise stiffeners riveted to the skin, typically 150 to 250 mm apart round the section. They stop the skin buckling between frames and carry the axial bending stress with it; on most airliners they do the whole job.

Longerons, where fitted, are fewer and heavier lengthwise members; they collect bending load at cut-outs and joints. The skin carries the shear from fuselage bending and torsion, part of the axial bending stress, and the cabin pressure as hoop tension.
Floor beams run across the cabin between frames and carry the floor and the passengers and cargo on it.
Pressure bulkheads close the pressurised cabin at the front and the rear. A pressurised fuselage is a pressure vessel, so both ends of the cabin must be sealed by a dome-shaped bulkhead.

blocks.text: A fuselage is also a beam: the tail unit loads the rear fuselage in bending and torsion, and the wing loads the centre section. Fuselage stresses are treated in Stress analysis of fuselage and tail unit.

Doors, windows, access panels and wheel wells cut skin out of the shell. A cut-out removes the material that was carrying the load, so the load must divert around the opening. The usual fix is a doubler: an extra plate riveted or bonded round the hole, thick enough to take the load the missing skin used to take. Corners of cut-outs are given a radius, because a sharp corner raises stress.

A wheel well is worse than a door, because it opens into the lower skin of the wing box itself, the part carrying tension in flight. Designers keep such holes as small as the mechanism allows, put them where the bending is low, and add heavy local reinforcement.

Shape is not cosmetic. The aerofoil section produces the lift and keeps drag low, so ribs and frames must hold it under load. Dents, wrinkles and bulges spoil the airflow and also lower the buckling strength of the panels, which is why handling damage near frames and stringers matters.

examples.question: A wing has a chord of 3.0 m along a spanwise length of 4.5 m from the root. The front spar lies at 15% chord and the rear spar at 60% chord. Ribs are placed at a pitch of 0.45 m. Find the width of the torsion box and the number of ribs.
steps: Front spar position: x<sub>front</sub> × c = 0.15 × 3.0 = 0.45 m from the leading edge.
Rear spar position: x<sub>rear</sub> × c = 0.60 × 3.0 = 1.80 m from the leading edge.
Box width: w<sub>box</sub> = 1.80 − 0.45 = 1.35 m, which is the same as (0.60 − 0.15) × 3.0 = 1.35 m.
Number of bays between ribs: 4.5 m ÷ 0.45 m = 10 bays.
Ribs: a bay has a rib at each end, and neighbouring bays share one. So there is a root rib, a tip rib at 4.5 m and 9 ribs between them: 10 bays need 10 + 1 = 11 ribs.
The torsion box is 1.35 m wide at every section where the chord is 3.0 m, and 11 ribs close 10 bays of 0.45 m each.
examples.answer: Torsion box width = 1.35 m; number of ribs = 11.

front_m = x<sub>front</sub> * c
rear_m = x<sub>rear</sub> * c
box = rear_m - front_m

ribs = int(round(bays)) + 1
print(round(box, 2))
print(int(round(bays)))
print(ribs)

traps: Counting bays as ribs: 10 bays need 11 ribs, because each end of a bay needs a rib.
Forgetting that a door, window or wheel well removes load-carrying skin and must be reinforced with a doubler.
Mixing up chord fractions with metres: 0.15 is a fraction of chord, 0.45 m is a length.
Swapping longeron and frame: longerons run lengthwise and take bending, frames are transverse rings that hold shape and pressure.
Thinking the skin alone bends the wing: the stringers and spar caps share the axial load.

quiz.q: What is a spar cap, and where does it sit?
quiz.a: A spanwise flange at the top or bottom of a spar web. It carries the axial load from wing bending.

quiz.q: Why is the closed cell between the two spars better at torsion than an open skin panel?
quiz.a: In a closed cell the shear has a continuous loop all round the section, so the whole loop shares the twisting load. An open sheet has no return path for the shear, so it twists and warps far more.

quiz.q: A wing has a chord of 2.4 m, spars at 12% and 62% chord, and ribs at 0.40 m pitch over a 3.6 m length. Find the box width and the number of ribs.
What are pressure bulkheads and where are they placed?
quiz.a: Dome-shaped walls that close the pressurised cabin at its forward and aft ends. They take the pressure end load.

quiz.q: Why are fuselage frames closely spaced while longerons are few and large?
quiz.a: Frames are there to hold the round shape and stop the thin skin from buckling and to help carry pressure hoop load, which needs short spacing. Longerons carry bending, which needs a large cross-sectional area far from the neutral axis, so a few heavy members are used.

quiz.q: A wheel well cuts into the lower skin of the wing box between the spars. What is lost and what must be added?
quiz.a: Part of the lower skin, which carries tension in flight and closes the torsion cell, is removed. The tension must be diverted into the surrounding skin and spar, usually by a doubler, thickened skin or a local beam, and the hole is given rounded corners and kept as small as possible. Torsion stiffness of the box also falls, so the remaining section must be checked.

quiz.q: Why does a sharp-cornered rectangular door opening need more reinforcement than a rounded one of the same size?
quiz.a: A sharp corner concentrates stress, so the local stress can be several times the nominal value and a crack can start there. A rounded corner spreads the diverted load over a longer length of skin, so the doubler and surrounding skin carry it at a lower stress.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, these layouts become finite element models: skin as shell elements, stringers and spar caps as rods or beams, ribs and frames as shear webs. Real wing boxes are sealed and used as fuel tanks, so the cut-outs and access panels also have to be leak-tight. Composite wings use fewer ribs, sometimes many metres apart, because the stiff skins tolerate larger unsupported panels.
